result.summary: The Messenians, settled at Naupactus, attack and capture Œniadæ in Acarnania. The Acarnanians then besiege them there, and after eight months the Messenians break out by night and escape to Naupactus with Ætolian help.

scenes.title: Messenians conquer Œniadæ
scenes.summary: Not content with Naupactus, the Messenians attack the Œniadæ, defeat them and besiege their fort until they surrender on terms.
scenes.stakes: The Œniadæ face capture, with their wives and children sold into slavery.

scenes.title: Acarnanians march on Œniadæ
scenes.summary: The Acarnanians give up a march on Naupactus and turn against the Messenians at Œniadæ. The Messenians decide to fight in the open.
scenes.stakes: The Messenians risk defeat and the loss of their new town and its supplies.

scenes.title: Battle before the gates
scenes.summary: The more numerous Acarnanians surround the Messenians, who break their lines repeatedly but are forced back; a blockade begins.
scenes.stakes: The Messenians risk being encircled and destroyed by greater numbers.

scenes.title: Night escape to Naupactus
scenes.summary: Provisions run out in the eighth month, and the Messenians slip out at night, fight through, and reach Naupactus with Ætolian help.
scenes.stakes: The Messenians face starvation and destruction while breaking through the enemy.

analysis.text: Courage set against numbers and luck: the exiled Messenians prove their valour but are finally overcome by supply shortage.
The episode shows the Messenian exiles in the 5th century BC trying to win land of their own, in the regional rivalries of Acarnania, Ætolia and Athens.

language_notes.text: "Shut them up in their fort" means they drove them back inside their fortified town and confined them there.
"Engines" are siege machines, such as battering rams, used to break down walls.
Marathon (490 BC): the Athenians beat the Persian invaders. "Medes" is the Greek habit of calling Persians Medes. A myriad is 10,000, so the figure is hugely exaggerated.
"Evenly poised" means the fight was evenly balanced, with neither side gaining a clear advantage.
"Flitting" means a stealthy departure. "First sleep" is an ancient way of naming the early part of the night.

context_notes.text: Œniadæ was a city in Acarnania, western Greece, on the river Achelous. It was long hostile to Athens.
Naupactus lay on the Gulf of Corinth. Athens had settled the exiled Messenians there, which is why they had a fleet.
The Messenians had lost their long wars against Sparta (the Lacedæmonians), and were exiles living far from home.

literary_notes.text: The Messenians are shown as proud and brave, losing only through bad luck, so the narrator casts them sympathetically.
"Came swarming up" likens the Acarnanians to insects, stressing their overwhelming numbers.
The Messenians boast their supplies would last ten years, yet they run out within eight months.
